source_read: PMC HTML (PMC7125061; CNS Drugs 2020;34(4):337-365), saved plain text of the PMC article page read start to end: abstract, Key Points, Introduction with Table 1 (DSM-5 criteria), Methods, Results (study selection and characteristics with Tables 2 and 3, Table 4 of all 43 trials, risk of bias across studies, outcomes and measures with Table 5, adherence, results of individual studies by drug class), Discussion (summary, reduction in use, withdrawal, setting, specific populations, limitations, future directions), Conclusions, acknowledgements, author contributions, funding, conflicts of interest and reference list. Figure 1 (PRISMA flow) is an image absent from the text; Supplementary materials 1-3 (search example, extended study table with trial-level risk-of-bias considerations, extracted data) were not available. The author-affiliation panel is collapsed in the saved text, so affiliations could not be read. No claim cites this source: step 2 (card check) only.

key_findings.correction: Numbers confirmed (Table 2 rows sum to 43 in each block). The publication range '1994 to 2019' is the card's correction of the text's '1995 and 2019' (reference 36 is dated 1994), as its note says.
Recomputed: 51/93 = 55% abstinence, 41/51 = 80% by urine, 10/93 = 11% craving, as printed.

Locator detail: the completion figures (38 trials, 2298 of 3733, 61.6%) are in the 2nd paragraph of Study Selection and Characteristics (the one after Table 2), the 70.3% men and nine men-only trials in the 3rd; women 29.7% and the 34 trials (79.1%) excluding psychiatric comorbidity are in Risk of Bias Within and Across Studies, 1st paragraph. 2298/3733 = 61.6% recomputed.
The four reference lists sum to 28 + 10 + 4 + 1 = 43 (recounted).

Signals were not confined to people with light baseline use: the Results (Antidepressants, 4th paragraph) also report a subgroup signal in male participants regardless of baseline use in Elkashef 2008 (higher proportion of MA-free weeks on bupropion), alongside the ORs 1.39 and 1.34 in men with low use and 1.27 in non-depressed women with low use; and Table 4 records a secondary finding in Heinzerling 2014 (more participants with negative urines on bupropion, with very low adherence). Suggested wording: 'signals were confined to post hoc, subgroup or secondary analyses (people with light baseline use, men) and to reduced cigarette smoking'.
Note: the text gives the sertraline trial as 14 weeks, Table 4 as 12 weeks (see reporting issue 4).

'Longer retention in one trial' follows Table 4 (Longo 2010: treatment arm retained longer); the Results text for the same trial says there was no significant difference between groups on its planned analyses, which it lists as including treatment retention, so the two parts of the review disagree on this point.

Two details: the statement that the implant trial shared the Swedish trial's positive amphetamine result is made in the Results (Opioid Antagonists, 2nd paragraph) as well as the Discussion (Reduction in Use, 3rd paragraph); and Table 4 shows that Kohno 2018 also used a 380 mg extended-release injection, so there were three extended-release injection trials, not the two the text names (references 29 and 56).

reporting_issues.note: Also, the Results (Opioid Agonists) say the buprenorphine-versus-methadone trial reduced craving 'compared with placebo', although Table 4 records that trial as having no control group.
32/183 = 17.4% recomputed; the text itself says this trial was not placebo controlled (10 mg imipramine as control).

All four conflicts are as described (amineptine: Table 4 'analysed as ITT' vs text 'completer analysis', 29 analysed; reference 24 ITT in Table 4 vs non-ITT list; reference 55 completer analysis in Table 4 but absent from the non-ITT list; reference 39 'NB' in Table 4 vs inside the double-blind range 24-45).
The positive attribution to the implant trial appears in the Results (Opioid Antagonists, 2nd paragraph) as well as in the Discussion.

All instances confirmed (the ondansetron text doses 0.5, 2 and 8 mg 'OD' are the daily totals of Table 4's 0.25, 1 and 4 mg twice daily). Two further instances: the sertraline trial runs 14 weeks in the text and 12 weeks in Table 4; and the Longo 2010 dexamphetamine trial is described in the text as showing no significant difference on planned analyses including retention, while Table 4 says the treatment arm was retained longer.
The Discussion's 'nearly a quarter' of trials without women corresponds to 9 of 43 (21%).

Review side confirmed (Discussion > Reduction in Use, 3rd paragraph: percentage of methamphetamine-negative urines over 12 weeks, results pending). The comparison with sc_trivedi_2021 is outside this source; it is consistent with the round-1 second reader's anchors for trivedi_2021 (response = at least 3 of 4 negative urines in the last 2 weeks of each stage).
The secondary-outcome block of Table 5 has the same misalignment ('participant satisfaction' measured by percentage completing medication and weeks in treatment).

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with AMSTAR 2 and with critically low confidence: items 2 (no protocol) and 7 (no list of excluded studies) are unambiguous critical flaws. Four item-level points, none of which changes the overall rating: (a) item 4 should be 'no', not 'partial yes': AMSTAR 2's partial yes needs at least two databases, the search strategy and a justification of publication restrictions, and the English-only restriction is not justified; (b) item 9 should be 'no' on the article's evidence: the Methods list allocation of participants, blinding of participants or personnel, sample, completion, analysis, overstated conclusions and funding, but not allocation concealment or outcome-assessor blinding, which AMSTAR 2 requires even for partial yes; if the editors read 'allocation' as covering concealment, the trial-level judgments are only in the unseen supplement and the METHODS extension would give 'no information' with a provisional rating; (c) item 13 offers only yes or no in AMSTAR 2, so 'partial yes' is not available; I would record 'yes' (the Discussion and Conclusions attribute the absence of convincing results to small, biased samples and low completion), with the card's point about the named signals kept in the note; (d) items 11, 12 and 15 should be recorded as 'no meta-analysis' rather than omitted, so the domain list is complete.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right: the bottom line (no medication with convincing results) matches the evidence, and the gaps concern the ranking of 'signals'. One addition to gap (3): the pexacerfont trial not only failed to separate amphetamine from opioid results, Table 4 also reports no difference in withdrawal (AWQ), yet the Discussion names pexacerfont as a withdrawal candidate. The card's funding note (an author of the review is an author of the lisdexamfetamine trial protocol, reference 68) is a fair flag for the 'agonist therapies show promise' conclusion.

missed: Bupropion in men: the Discussion (Reduction in Use, 5th paragraph) attributes the signal in people with light baseline use or in men to Shoptaw 2008 (reference 60) alone, whereas the Results attribute the male-subgroup finding to Elkashef 2008 (reference 33). Minor misattribution; claims about a bupropion effect in men should cite Elkashef 2008 directly.

Amineptine market status: the review says amineptine was never FDA-approved and 'has been suspended in other jurisdictions' for liver toxicity and liability for non-medical use, with no date and no reference (Results > Antidepressants, 1st paragraph). Relevant to cl_meth_withdrawal_medication, whose 1999 withdrawal date rests on acheson_2023: this same-group review does not corroborate the date.
